1211.quote_or_event: “If only someone would come, and lead me to meet my Darling Beloved; I would sell myself to him.”
1211.explanation: Guru Ram Das, speaking as the longing soul-bride, says she would give herself away to whoever brings her Beloved to meet her.
1211.tie_back: The Kural's wife wonders what feast could repay the dream that brought word of her husband; the Guru's bride likewise has nothing smaller to offer such a go-between than her whole self.
1211.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1211._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on boundless gratitude to whoever brings the beloved near, though the go-between in Gurbani is the Guru or a saint, not a dream, and the love is spiritual, not romantic.

1212.quote_or_event: “This night, I did not sleep with my Husband Lord, and now my body is suffering in pain. Go and ask the deserted bride, how she passes her night.”
1212.explanation: Sheikh Farid speaks as a bride kept from her Husband Lord for a single night, and says only a deserted wife knows how such nights are survived.
1212.tie_back: The Kural's wife begs her eyes to sleep so that she can tell her beloved in a dream how barely she has lived through his absence; Farid's bride likewise wants someone to hear how the night of separation is endured.
1212.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 30) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1212._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), both lines of salok 30; reasonable fit on telling the pain of nights apart, but Farid has no motif of sleep as a way to reach the beloved, and the Husband here is God, a spiritual rather than romantic love.

1213.quote_or_event: “In a dream, I was lifted up; why didn't I grasp the hem of His Robe?”
1213.explanation: Guru Arjan's soul-bride recalls rising to meet her Lord in a dream, the only place she glimpsed Him, and reproaches herself for not holding on.
1213.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that he who shows no grace while she is awake is still seen in her dreams, and that this keeps her alive; the Guru's bride too has her Lord only in a dream.
1213.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1362, Phunhay, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1213._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a genuine dream-meeting in the bride-soul idiom, but the stress falls on regret at not grasping the Lord rather than on the dream sustaining life, and the love is spiritual, not romantic.

1214.quote_or_event: “... the friendly True Guru has come into my dream beautifully attired and adored.”
1214.explanation: In one of his Kabits Bhai Gurdas describes the True Guru coming to him in a dream, dressed in beauty, so that the meeting denied in waking life happens in sleep.
1214.tie_back: The Kural says love's joy comes in dreams because the dream seeks out and brings the one who will not come by day; Bhai Gurdas likewise receives his Beloved through a dream.
1214.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabit Savaiye, Kabit 205 (English translation as given on BaniDB)
1214._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (opening words of the translated line omitted); Bhai Gurdas's Kabits are revered early exegesis, not scripture, and the Beloved here is the Guru, a spiritual not romantic love.

1215.quote_or_event: “The world is a drama, staged in a dream. In a moment, the play is played out.”
1215.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that worldly life is as passing as a dream, a show that ends in a moment.
1215.tie_back: The Kural's wife finds that seeing her husband awake was sweet only while it lasted, just like seeing him in a dream; Gurbani goes further and calls waking life itself a dream that is over in a moment.
1215.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 18, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1215._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the Kural's levelling of waking and dreaming as equally brief, but Guru Nanak's point is detachment from a passing world, not the sweetness of love.

1216.quote_or_event: “Enjoying the bliss of divine dream, I was woken up by the voice of rain-bird and that broke my celestial dream. The awe and marvel of love-filled state disappeared reawakening the pangs of separation. I was restless like a fish out of water.”
1216.explanation: Bhai Gurdas describes a dream of union with the Guru broken by the call of the rain-bird, so that waking brings back the pain of separation.
1216.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that if there were no such thing as waking, her beloved would never leave her; in Bhai Gurdas it is exactly the moment of waking that ends the meeting and leaves the lover like a fish out of water.
1216.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabit Savaiye, Kabit 205 (English translation as given on BaniDB)
1216._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB; near one-to-one on waking as the thief of a dream-union, but this is Bhai Gurdas's exegetical poetry, not scripture, and the love is for the Guru, spiritual rather than romantic.

1217.quote_or_event: “In a dream, He came, and went away again; I cried so many tears.”
1217.explanation: Guru Nanak's soul-bride says her Lord visited her in a dream and left again, and she was left weeping.
1217.tie_back: The Kural's wife asks why the hard-hearted one who will not come while she is awake visits her dreams only to torment her; Guru Nanak's bride feels the same pain of a dream-visit that ends in tears.
1217.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 558, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1217._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); near one-to-one on a dream-visit that leaves the beloved in tears, though Guru Nanak never calls the Lord cruel, and the love is spiritual, not romantic.

1218.quote_or_event: “When I look within my being, I find that my Beloved is with me.”
1218.explanation: Guru Arjan's bride-soul discovers that the Beloved she longs for is not far off but present inside her.
1218.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her husband rests on her shoulders while she sleeps and slips into her heart the moment she wakes; Guru Arjan likewise finds the Beloved dwelling within, never truly absent.
1218.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1095, Raag Maaroo, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1218._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on the beloved who lives in the heart, though the Kural's playful sleeping-and-waking contrast is absent and the Beloved is God, a spiritual rather than romantic love.

1219.quote_or_event: “Even in her dreams, she does not meet her Husband Lord.”
1219.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the self-willed soul-bride who is so far from God that she does not meet Him even in her dreams.
1219.tie_back: The Kural's wife says only women who never see their lovers in dreams blame men who stay away; Guru Amar Das likewise singles out the bride who does not meet her Husband even in dreams as the truly forsaken one.
1219.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 127, Raag Maajh, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1219._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa, second half of the verse); reasonable fit on not meeting the beloved even in dreams as the mark of real separation, but Guru Amar Das is condemning the self-willed soul, not defending a husband, and the love is spiritual.

1220.quote_or_event: “The miracle of a dream is known to the one who has seen it. No one else can see it. Then how can anyone else know about it?”
1220.explanation: Bhai Gurdas uses the dream as an image for the Sikh's private meeting with the Guru, which outsiders cannot see or judge.
1220.tie_back: The Kural's wife answers the town's gossip that her husband has abandoned her by asking whether they cannot see him coming to her in dreams; Bhai Gurdas agrees that what happens in a dream is known only to the one who sees it.
1220.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabit Savaiye, Kabit 305 (English translation as given on BaniDB)
1220._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB; strong fit on the dreamer's knowledge that onlookers cannot share, but this is Bhai Gurdas's exegetical poetry, not scripture, and its subject is the Guru-Sikh union, spiritual rather than romantic.
